source.title: Benefits of Early Stopping in Gradient Descent for Overparameterized Logistic Regression
source.authors: Jingfeng Wu; Peter L. Bartlett; Matus Telgarsky; Bin Yu

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices; no apparent truncation.
record.tranche_reason: The paper proves generalization bounds for early-stopped gradient descent and lower bounds for interpolating estimators in overparameterized logistic regression. It does not test the listed versions’ specific interventions or settings.
record.gate_note: The paper reports theoretical results for well-specified logistic regression, not a comparison of networks trained on natural versus random labels. Its Figure 1 describes training and population risks along a GD path, but supplies no numerical values in the text.
record.test_reason: The study proves results about early stopping, calibration, and interpolation in logistic regression. None tests V1–V8: fitting noisy logistic-regression data does not establish V1's random-versus-natural-label comparison, and changing stopping time does not test V2's width dependence.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate with its stated qualifications. Oracle-tuned early stopping yields calibration and consistency under well-specification; asymptotic GD has unbounded logistic risk and positive calibration error, although it may remain classification-consistent. Under additional conditions, interpolators require exponentially many samples for small excess classification error compared with polynomial guarantees for early stopping. The authors also establish conditional connections between GD and ℓ2-regularization paths.
record.recipe_differences: Theoretical analysis of gradient descent for overparameterized logistic regression; no random-label experiment or neural-network architecture comparison.
record.method_sensitivity: The results distinguish early stopping from convergence and depend on data assumptions; the zero-one lower bound additionally requires sparsity and specified covariance-rank conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: Oracle-tuned early-stopped GD has vanishing excess logistic risk under the stated assumptions, whereas asymptotic GD has divergent logistic risk and positive limiting calibration error.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Early stopping can ensure calibration and logistic-risk consistency in well-specified overparameterized logistic regression where asymptotic GD lacks these properties.

fits_no_version.finding: Under additional sparsity, signal-norm, and covariance-rank conditions, every interpolating estimator has excess classification error at least of order 1/sqrt(ln(n) ln(1/δ)).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In specified noisy overparameterized logistic-regression problems, interpolation requires exponentially many samples for small excess classification error, whereas suitably early-stopped GD can require only polynomially many.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 267 (2025)
record.problems: The early-stopping bound uses an oracle-chosen stopping time that depends on the true parameter. The zero-one lower bound applies only under additional sparsity and covariance-rank assumptions. Figure 1 has no numerical results in the supplied text.

untested.parts: Matched random-label fitting and natural-label held-out accuracy, including chance-level held-out accuracy with random labels.
Test error as network width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning budgets and recovery recipes.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove the penalty.
Dropout's effect on held-out error across training-set sizes and augmentation regimes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, its correlation with generalization gaps, and comparisons with other measures.
Accuracy after removing highly memorized training examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Figure 1 varies optimization length at fixed dimension and sample size; its deterioration after interpolation does not test width-dependent double descent. No results bearing on V1–V8 are missing from the rows.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label memorization or natural-label generalization comparison; no listed architectures or experiments.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold experiment.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
No removal of memorized training examples.

rows.subject: Gradient descent (GD), early-stopped; overparameterized logistic regression
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 3.1 bounds population excess logistic risk at an oracle-chosen stopping time.

conditions.value: Well-specified logistic regression with anisotropic Gaussian design

rows.uncertainty: Probability at least 1 − δ; bound stated up to ≲
rows.note: The stopping time depends on oracle information about w*; the paper says this is not a practical algorithm.
rows.check: The theoretical bound is correctly recorded but measures none of the listed versions. Its guarantee also requires the stepsize bound in Theorem 3.1; overparameterization is an intended setting rather than a necessary assumption of this theorem.

rows.subject: Gradient descent (GD) at convergence; overparameterized logistic regression
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 4.1 bounds population logistic risk and calibration error for diverging estimators whose directions converge; the authors state this applies to GD iterates.
rows.measure: Population logistic risk and calibration error
rows.baseline: Bayes logistic risk min L; calibration target 0
rows.uncertainty: Theorem states a constant C > 1; no statistical uncertainty interval
rows.note: This concerns logistic risk and calibration; it does not establish the listed claim’s random-label/natural-label comparison.
rows.check: The stated risk divergence and calibration lower bound match Theorem 4.1, but neither measures a listed version. Logistic-risk inconsistency must not be interpreted as classification inconsistency.

rows.subject: Interpolating estimators, including asymptotic GD; overparameterized logistic regression
rows.size_stated: Overparameterized; rank(Σ)/[n ln(n) ln(1/δ)] bounded between C1 and C2
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 4.2 gives a lower bound on excess zero-one error for every interpolating estimator under stated sparsity and sample-size conditions.

conditions.value: Well-specified logistic regression; Σ1/2w* is k-sparse

rows.uncertainty: Probability at least 1 − δ; bound stated up to ≳
rows.note: A lower bound on excess error, not a reported chance-level comparison or a claim that zero-one error fails to converge.
rows.check: The lower bound matches Theorem 4.2 but measures none of the listed versions, so 'partial' is inappropriate. Add the omitted condition 1/C1 ≤ ||w*||Σ ≤ C1. The bound decreases with sample size and does not establish asymptotically nonvanishing classification error.
